title: DeepSeek's retrained V4-Flash beats the lab's own flagship on nine agent benchmarks — with no architecture change
subtitle: Same 284B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts structure, same 13B active per token, same 1M context — and roughly double the agent scores, undercutting the field on price.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: DeepSeek released the official public beta of its V4-Flash API on July 31 under the build designation V4-Flash-0731, and the accompanying benchmarks landed the same day with a single unusual detail: the lab did not change the model's architecture. Same 284-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts structure as the preview build it replaces, same ~13B active parameters per token, same 1-million-token context window. The gains — and they are large — came from retraining alone. Terminal Bench 2.1 climbs from 61.8 on the Flash preview to 82.7 on 0731. DeepSWE rises from 7.3 to 54.4. On all nine agent and coding benchmarks DeepSeek published, the 0731 build scores higher than DeepSeek's own V4-Pro-Preview, which uses more compute and costs more per token.

The pricing puts the model at the front of the price-performance frontier. DeepSeek V4-Flash-0731 lists at $0.14 per 1M input tokens and $0.28 per 1M output tokens on the DeepSeek API — roughly a fifth of what OpenAI charges for GPT-5.6 Luna after its 80% cut last week, and closer to a tenth of what Anthropic charges for a Claude Opus 5 call. Independent benchmarks are still being posted; the numbers above are the vendor's own, and the field will spend the next week reproducing them on private evaluation suites before drawing firm conclusions. The historical DeepSeek pattern of overclaiming and then being confirmed within a fortnight suggests the gains are directionally real even if the exact numbers move.

The interesting mechanism is that a retrain of an unchanged architecture can roughly double a model's agent scores. What DeepSeek published points to two ingredients: a larger and more agent-specific post-training set — trajectory data from real tool-use sessions rather than static instruction-tuning corpora — and reinforcement learning against verifiable outcomes on coding and terminal tasks, closing the loop that agent benchmarks actually measure. Neither is novel. Both were reported by Anthropic, OpenAI and Google over the past year. What DeepSeek is demonstrating, again, is that a well-executed post-training pass on a mid-sized MoE can move the frontier as much as a new architecture would, at a fraction of the training-compute bill.

For learners: if you evaluate models for a coding, agent or long-horizon task, do not skip the low-price open-weight tier. The gap between a $0.14-per-million-input frontier open-weight model and a $2-per-million-input closed frontier model is now often within the noise of your own evaluation suite, and the price differential compounds hard once you start running agents in loops. The correct discipline is to build a small, honest eval on your actual task, run it against three or four models across price tiers, and let the numbers on your suite — not the vendor's leaderboard — decide. That habit is going to matter more, not less, over the next year as the pace of retraining announcements keeps accelerating.
